title: Records they listened to in 1926: Armstrong, Henderson, Goldkette, Bix
summary: Phillips lists Louis Armstrong's Hot Five, Fletcher Henderson, Jean Goldkette, Red Nichols, Trumbauer, Bix and Goodman as what everyone was hearing.

bands.name: Red Nichols and His Five Pennies

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Before you go into the Minneapolis dance band time, let me ask you this. This is already 1926 going into 1927. So what kind of music were you listening to at that time? What kind of influences were going on with your musical development? What kind of records and what kind of...?
Louis Armstrong He was hot then, with that Hot Five. And Fletcher Henderson, the big band...
You listened to Fletcher Henderson's big band?
These were records that you could get and you could listen to them.
What kinds of things was Lester listening to? Well, what else were you listening to, first of all?
Well, that was the general kind of music that everybody listened to. Then the band that everybody listened to was Jean Goldkette.
Did you own a record player at that time?
Yeah, we had plenty of records. Red Nichols. Frankie Trumbauer. Bix. Benny Goodman. This was all in '26...
I know some of those records, like "Singing The Blues," that didn't come out until '27, I think.
Yeah. Well, all of them was... But they had some more out, though, before that time. Like "Davenport Blues." Then after Bix got with Paul Whiteman, we used to listen to him a lot, you know.
So these were the records you were listening to.

That's what everybody was listening to then. All the trumpet players were listening to Bix and Louis, because about 1926 and 1927 and on through there, that's when they was hot. I mean, the records... Wasn't like
